discovery: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated many-body physics with ultracold atoms in optical lattices

nominees.name: Immanuel Bloch
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics and Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Germany

nominees.name: Peter Zoller
nominees.affiliation: University of Innsbruck and IQOQI, Austrian Academy of Sciences, Austria

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum many-body physics
motivation: Feynman proposed using one quantum system to emulate another. Zoller and Jaksch showed that ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters. In 2002 Greiner and Bloch observed the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator quantum phase transition, which turned that proposal into a working experimental paradigm. Both then developed quantum gas microscopes that image and control single atoms at individual lattice sites. With these tools they observed antiferromagnetic correlations in the Fermi-Hubbard model, many-body localization, string order and entanglement dynamics. These questions are hard for classical computation and theory to settle. Their work made analog quantum simulation a quantitative experimental science, and dozens of laboratories now use it to study strongly correlated matter, magnetism and non-equilibrium dynamics. It also laid foundations for neutral-atom quantum computing. This is a defining achievement of twenty-first-century physics.
